heading: Medicines, birch sap and sea ice
intro: Dissolving, concentration and the effect of temperature are part of everyday work on the land for many First Nations and Inuit communities. These connections come from Cree lands at Edmonton, a Woodland Cree birch syrup camp in Treaty 8 and Inuit sea ice in Nunatsiavut. Each one links to the solutions, concentrations and solubility you explore in this lab.

peoples: Cree: the maskêkosak of Enoch Cree Nation (maskêkosihk)
connections.title: maskêkosihk: the Land of Medicines
connections.text: Big Island lies in the North Saskatchewan River valley in southwest Edmonton. A Government of Alberta fact sheet says the traditional lands of the maskêkosak, the people of the Land of Medicines, encompassed Big Island. Their lands are known as maskêkosihk, or Enoch Cree Nation, in Treaty No. 6 Territory. The fact sheet says plants provided plentiful remedies, and some say more than 200 medicines were gathered and used. Making a plant tea is one kind of dissolving: hot water draws substances out of leaves. The Cree Literacy Network says that in Saskatchewan and Alberta, Labrador tea is known as maskêkopakwa, muskeg tea.

sources.title: Government of Alberta: Big Island cultural values fact sheet (2022). Source of the Cree names maskêkosihk (the Land of Medicines) and maskêkosak (people of the Land of Medicines)
maskêkosak newowacistwan nâtamâkêwin society (Enoch Cree Nation): About. Source of maskêkosihk as the Cree name for Enoch, and its place in Treaty No. 6 Territory
Cree Literacy Network: Muskeg Tea. Source of the Cree name maskêkopakwa (muskeg tea, Labrador tea) used in Saskatchewan and Alberta

connections.title: waskwayâpoy: birch sap becomes syrup
connections.text: Woodland Cree First Nation, in the Peace River region and Treaty 8, makes syrup from waskwayâpoy (birch sap) each spring. An Alberta Historic Places article written with the Nation describes Knowledge Keepers Nancy Williams and Sara Williams tapping birch trees, with Elders, youth and community members taking part. A tapped birch is left to rest for at least three seasons. The sap is strained and simmered over low heat, so water evaporates and the sugar becomes more concentrated. Birch sap holds much less sugar than maple sap. The article says birch takes about 120 parts sap for one part syrup, compared with about 40 to 1 for maple.

sources.title: Alberta Historic Places RETROactive: Season of the Birch: Continuing Practices of Woodland Cree First Nation (2024, written in collaboration with Woodland Cree First Nation). Source of the Cree name waskwayâpoy (birch sap)

connections.title: Sikuk: sea ice that pushes out salt
connections.text: Chaim Christiana Andersen, from Nain, Nunatsiavut, wrote with Geoff Rayner-Canham in the chemistry magazine Chem 13 News about Sikuk (sea ice). He explains that Inuit use sea ice mainly for transportation. As sea water freezes, dissolved salt particles are pushed out, so the ice itself is essentially fresh water. In spring, freshwater pools form on its surface, and a photo shows him going to imittak (fetch water). In the Indigenous Peoples Atlas of Canada, Joey Angnatok of Nain and Rodd Laing of the Nunatsiavut Government write that pockets of brine form within sea ice, and that Inuktut has dozens of words for sea ice.

sources.title: University of Waterloo, Chem 13 News (reprint of February 2019 issue): Chemistry and Inuit Life and Culture: Sea ice, essential for northern survival, by Chaim Christiana Andersen and Geoff Rayner-Canham. Source of the Inuttitut words Sikuk (sea ice) and imittak (fetch water)
Indigenous Peoples Atlas of Canada: Sea ice, by Joey Angnatok and Rodd Laing

try: Woodland Cree First Nation simmers birch sap until it becomes syrup. If 120 L of sap makes about 1 L of syrup, did the mass of sugar change, or only the amount of water? Use the words dilute, concentrated and evaporate to explain. The article warns that too strong a boil can evaporate all the water. What would be left behind?

When sea water freezes, dissolved salt is pushed out of the ice. Predict how the concentration of the salt water just under new sea ice compares with ordinary sea water. Link your answer to the brine pockets that Angnatok and Laing describe, and to crystallization in Lesson 6.

Labrador tea, or maskêkopakwa, is one of many plants made into tea. Using a store bought tea bag, plan a fair test of how water temperature affects how quickly the colour spreads. Which variable do you change, which do you measure and which must stay the same? Is this a test of rate of dissolving, or of solubility?

slide.title: Medicines, birch sap and sea ice
points: Edmonton: Big Island was part of maskêkosihk, the Land of Medicines, lands of Enoch Cree Nation.
Alberta: Woodland Cree First Nation simmers waskwayâpoy (birch sap) to concentrate it into syrup.
Canada: Inuit in Nunatsiavut know Sikuk (sea ice), which pushes out salt as it freezes.
slide.notes: Use the Edmonton point with Lesson 2 (dissolving: a plant tea is hot water dissolving substances from leaves). Use the Alberta point with Lesson 4 (concentration: evaporating water makes a solution more concentrated, the opposite of diluting). Use the Canada point with Lesson 6 (temperature and crystallization: as water freezes, salt is left behind in the liquid). Point students to the Ways of knowing section in the lab for sources and discussion prompts. Do not ask students to harvest or prepare wild plants.

review_flags: Existing content: the only Indigenous reference in the lab and deck is the footer line "Edmonton, Treaty 6 territory." It has no citation. The Enoch society page and the Canadian Heritage Rivers page already used in another draft could support it if you want one. Not Indigenous, but also unsourced: Lesson 5's Fort Saskatchewan salt cavern example and the trout and cold water note.

Names used and their sources: maskêkosihk and maskêkosak (Government of Alberta Big Island fact sheet, which glosses them "the Land of Medicines" and "people of the Land of Medicines"; the Enoch society page writes "People of the land of Medicine" and also spells it Maskekosihk); maskêkopakwa (Cree Literacy Network); waskwayâpoy (Alberta Historic Places article written with Woodland Cree First Nation); Sikuk and imittak (Andersen and Rayner-Canham, who call the language Inuttitut; the Atlas uses Inuktut). I did not use nêhiyaw or nêhiyawak in the peoples fields because no fetched source defines it; the Enoch society page uses nêhiyawak without a gloss. Would you like "nêhiyaw (Cree)" added to match other drafts?

The Big Island fact sheet is Government of Alberta, not Enoch Cree Nation, and it speaks in the past tense ("once encompassed Big Island"). I kept that wording for the land but avoided past tense for the people. Would you like to ask Enoch Cree Nation, or invite an Enoch Knowledge Keeper, to confirm this framing and whether they want Big Island named in a classroom lab?

The Cree Literacy Network muskeg tea post reproduces an Elder's account from Norway House, Manitoba, that includes a medicinal use. I used only the plant name and the Saskatchewan and Alberta naming note, and left out all preparation and health content on purpose. The tea prompt uses a store bought tea bag, not a wild plant. Is that acceptable?

The Edmonton connection joins two sources: Big Island and maskêkosihk (Edmonton specific) and the name maskêkopakwa (Alberta wide). No source says that Labrador tea grows on or is gathered at Big Island, and the text does not claim it. Please check the wording does not imply that.

Birch syrup: "about 120 parts sap for one part syrup" is my plain language reading of the article's "approximately 120:1" (birch) and "approximately 40:1" (maple). Please confirm. The article is by Laura Golebiowski (Government of Alberta Indigenous Consultation Adviser) "in collaboration with Woodland Cree First Nation." Would you like to contact the Nation or its Traditional Lands Manager before naming Nancy Williams and Sara Williams to students?

Sea ice: the chemistry explanation (salt pushed out as ice forms) is presented in Chem 13 News as chemistry, written by an Inuk author from Nain with a chemist co-author. It is not presented as traditional knowledge, and my text does not call it that. Whether Inuit have their own terms for salty new ice versus fresh old ice I could not confirm from a fetched source: the SIKU and WHOI glossary pages did not show terms in text. If you want an Inuktut term for salty or fresh ice, I would need to keep looking (SIKU Ice and Snow Profiles).

I did not include a Métis or Niitsitapi connection. I found no well sourced Métis or Blackfoot example tied to dissolving or concentration in this session (searches on Métis birch syrup and Indigenous led water quality monitoring near Edmonton did not yield a fetchable, specific source). Would you like me to research one further, for example Métis plant knowledge or a salt lick or mineral spring?
